extracted.intended_audience: poets, orators, and students of rhetoric (writers and critics interested in achieving the Sublime)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and recognizing the literary Sublime in poetry, prose, and oratory: its sources, the faults that corrupt it, and practical stylistic and structural methods to attain it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombast/grandiloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: Bombast is a common fault in aspiring lofty writers: excessive, hollow bulk of language that transcends the Sublime and becomes ludicrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that writers who fear appearing feeble often slide into the opposite extreme of bombast; such grandiloquence produces confusion and obscurity rather than energy. Examples: inflated phrases like “curling torrent flames” become burlesque when they exceed genuine force. Remedy: prefer genuine force of thought over mere swelling diction; test phrases for whether they sustain actual terror or grandeur when examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid puerility (pedantic over-elaboration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Puerility is the failure of feeble and narrow minds—an over-elaboration that ends in frigidity and silly affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors aiming at brilliancy or polish may lapse into paltriness. The treatise labels this the most ignoble vice in writing and contrasts it with true grandeur. Practical sign: ornamentation that reads as cleverness rather than power; fix by pruning affected little conceits that distract from the core idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false sentiment (ill‑timed or empty emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: False sentiment is an ill-timed and empty display of emotion: feeling where no emotion is called for or emotion greater than the situation warrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such displays leave readers cold and produce tedious personal feeling unconnected with the subject. The author advises separate treatment of the pathetic but flags false sentiment as a vice to be avoided: ensure emotional displays are warranted, connected to subject-matter, and proportionate to situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frigidity and childish conceits
rubrics_metrics.description: Frigidity manifests as coldness, childish absurdities, and strained attempts at novelty or striking turns of phrase that are inappropriate or absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include strange or misplaced comparisons (e.g., comparing Alexander to Isocrates) and whimsical expressions that expose want of judgment. Frigidity often arises from eagerness to be striking; remedy by self-critique and removing forced or juvenile conceits.

rubrics_metrics.name: True Sublime: lasting, pregnant, and universally affecting
rubrics_metrics.description: The True Sublime is that quality of language and thought which is 'pregnant in suggestion', impossible to distract from, takes strong and lasting hold on memory, and pleases and elevates readers across differences of taste and condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests for true sublimity: (a) under repeated judgment by an acute critic it continues to elevate the mind; (b) it suggests ideas beyond what is expressed; (c) the longer you read it the more it impresses, not lessens; (d) it produces a consistent impression across varied readers. If a passage fails these tests it is a false or specious sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur of thought (first principal source)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lofty cast of mind—greatness of conception and generous spirit—is the primary source of sublimity; it is mainly a natural faculty though it can be cultivated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublime thought often belongs to high minds; training the soul with noble thoughts helps. Examples: Homeric passages, the opening of the Jewish Law (“God said…”) and lofty conceptions that measure things by vast scales. Practical implication: aim to think in large, majestic terms; orient subject-matter toward genuinely elevated ideas rather than ornament alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigorous and spirited treatment of the passions (second principal source)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appropriate, genuine, and vigorous treatment of passions contributes strongly to sublimity; passion used rightly can produce a 'fine madness' effect conducive to sublime expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But not all passions are sublime—some (pity, grief, fear) may be low—so choose passions that elevate and avoid confusing pathos with sublimity. In oratory, panegyric and declamatory passages often require dignity and sublimity whereas pathos may be absent. Use passion to uplift and energize, not merely to evoke cheap sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artifice in the employment of figures (figures of thought and speech) (third principal source)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate artifice—figures of thought and figures of speech—helps produce sublimity when used skillfully and not for mere novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures should serve grandeur: metaphors, hyperboles, plurals for singulars, and other ornaments can aid sublimity but also cause failure if misused. The author distinguishes figures that aid true sublimity from those that are mere frippery; learn the types and apply with restraint and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignified expression: proper choice of words and metaphors (fourth principal source)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dignified expression consists of selecting the proper words and using metaphors and ornaments of diction that convey loftiness without affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes lexical choices, use of metaphors, and other diction-level devices. Examples: the difference between stirring, apt metaphors and high‑flown conceits that become ludicrous. Practical counsel: prefer words stamped with the peculiar force of the scene; avoid frigid or flashy vocabulary not justified by the thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majesty and elevation of structure (fifth principal source)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity arises also from large-scale structural elevation: majesty and an elevated organization of whole passages or works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This involves the choice and ordering of constituent parts into a solid, uniform edifice of sublimity—ascending amplification, coherent selection of striking incidents, and avoidance of patched or gaping composition. Work on macro-architecture as well as local diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and combination of the most striking circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: One cause of sublimity is choosing the most striking circumstances of the subject and combining them into one animate whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should pick vivid, characteristic signs (Sappho's list of bodily symptoms of love, Homer's tempest features) and weld them together, rejecting whatever is not essential. Avoid introducing frivolous or tiresome details that mar the unified effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplification: gather and present material in a rising scale supported by sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplification consists in bringing forward one impressive point after another in a continuous and ascending scale; it gives extension where sublimity gives elevation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amplification is useful in many modes—exaggeration, argument emphasis, disposition of actions or passions—but it is incomplete without sublimity (except when aiming only to excite pity or degrade an opponent). Use amplification for perorations, descriptive passages, history, and digressions, but ensure the presence of sublimity so the piece retains soul and avoids diffuseness without force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pursuing novelty for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: The pursuit of novelty in thought and expression often leads to glaring improprieties of language and to absurdities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornaments and novel turns often form the origin of both excellence and failure. The text cautions against novelty that sacrifices coherence and taste; prefer tested, noble expressions and deliberate innovation only when it strengthens thought and feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ vivid, imaginative images fitting the purpose (poetic vs oratorical aims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Images should be vivid and produced by the speaker's imagined vision: poets aim to astound; orators to give perspicuity—both to work on the emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Erinyes passages and Homer's grand images. Good images are those where the author 'sees' what he speaks of and compels the reader likewise; tailor images to genre: poetical images should astonish, oratorical images should clarify argument and move feeling without grotesque excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate great masters as disciplined inspiration (not plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emulous imitation of great poets and prose-writers (Homer, Plato, Demosthenes, Thucydides) is recommended as a way to learn sublimity; this is not plagiarism but copying from fair forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use models as beacons to guide style and elevate thought; imagine how the greats would judge and let that audience discipline your craft. Practically: study exemplary passages, adopt their large compositional ideas, and measure your work against them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match diction and syntactic shape to emotional/scene constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Force the language—choice of prepositions, combinations, and syntax—to imitate and reflect the peculiar anxiety or agitation of the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Homer’s combination of opposite prepositions to 'torture' language so it imitates the agony of a tempest. Practical tip: let grammatical and syntactic choices mirror the felt dynamics of the subject; these formal manipulations should arise from, and reinforce, the emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prune non‑essential, frivolous, or unbecoming details
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything frivolous, unbecoming, or tiresome interposed among the vivid features will mar the general effect and give a patched, gaping appearance to the structure of sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be fastidious about rejecting anything not essential to the subject; aim for a solid, uniform composition. The text contrasts weaker descriptions (Aratus) that limit peril with Homer who leaves danger unlimited—avoid specifying mitigating details that reduce grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect decorum and avoid impious or indecent excesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity should not overstep bounds of decency or become impious; descriptions that degrade the divine or violate propriety undermine grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 'Battle of the Gods' in Homer may be 'downright impious' by overstepping decorum. Test sublime passages against standards of decency appropriate to their subject and audience; preserve the dignity of divine or heroic subjects.
